summaries.example: Imagine a game about the sentence, “If the box has a red ball and a blue ball, then it has a red ball.” One player says the whole sentence. The other may ask about the first part of the “if.” The first player must then answer. Next, the other player can ask for one part of “red ball and blue ball.” If the red-ball part is requested, the first player can answer with “the box has a red ball.” The winner is the player who still has a legal move when the other player has none.
summaries.summary: Dialogical logic studies reasoning as a conversation with rules. Two players discuss a thesis, or main statement. One player supports it, while the other tests it by asking for challenges or reasons. A play is made of moves, and the rules say which moves are allowed. Rules for words such as “and” and “if” explain how those statements can be challenged and defended. Other rules control the order of play and how it ends. In the standard approach, the proponent may use a simple statement only after the opponent has brought it into the dialogue. A single play can be won because the other player made an unhelpful choice. A winning strategy is stronger: it is a complete plan that succeeds no matter how the opponent plays. The approach can also change its rules to study other systems of logic, including classical and modal logic. Later versions try to make reasons and the content of simple statements more explicit.
key_ideas: Dialogical logic explains meaning by looking at how people use statements while they challenge and defend them.
The two players follow rules. Some rules explain how particular words work, such as “and,” “or,” and “if.”
Other rules explain the larger shape of the game, including whose turn it is and when the game ends.
Winning one particular play is different from having a plan that wins against every possible move by the other player.
Different rule choices can create different kinds of logic.
summaries.why_it_matters: This approach shows that logic is not only about symbols on a page. It can also be about asking, answering, challenging, and giving reasons. Thinking in games helps us notice the difference between a lucky answer and a reliable plan. It also shows how changing rules can change the kind of reasoning being studied.

important_terms.definition: A way of studying logic by treating arguments as rule-governed conversations or games.
A person who puts forward the main statement that the dialogue is about.
A person who questions or challenges the main statement.
A permitted action in the dialogue, such as making a statement, asking a question, challenging, or answering.
A plan that tells a player what to do for every possible choice the other player might make.

questions_to_think_about: Why might asking questions help us understand what a statement means?
How is winning one game different from having a plan for every game?
Should a player be allowed to introduce a new fact that the other player has not mentioned?

summaries.example: Consider the thesis p ∨ ¬p, read as “p or not-p.” In the intuitionistic dialogical framework, the opponent asks the proponent to choose a side. If the proponent chooses ¬p, the opponent may state p and leave the proponent without a defence. The proponent cannot simply return to the earlier choice, because the intuitionistic game rule requires attention to the latest unanswered challenge. In a classical dialogue, that restriction is removed. After the opponent states p, the proponent may answer the earlier disjunction challenge by choosing p, so the same thesis can be won under the classical structural rules. summaries.summary: Dialogical logic explains logical meaning and reasoning through regulated argument games. In the standard Lorenzen–Lorenz framework, a proponent states a thesis and an opponent challenges it. Particle rules specify the appropriate challenge and defence for each logical constant. A conjunction can be challenged by requesting either conjunct, whereas a disjunction is defended by the player who chooses a disjunct. Structural rules govern the overall organization of the play, including repetition limits and which unanswered challenge must be addressed. The play level concerns individual sequences of interaction; the strategy level concerns a complete plan across all possible plays. This distinction matters because a proponent may win a particular play only because the opponent chose poorly, while validity requires a winning strategy against every permitted response. Intuitionistic and classical dialogue games preserve the same local rules but differ in a structural rule controlling the transfer and reuse of information. The framework has also been extended toward dialogical pluralism, modal logics, and approaches that make reasons and content more explicit.
key_ideas: In the Lorenzen and Lorenz tradition, meaning is treated pragmatically: it is connected to what players may do with an expression in a dialogue.
Particle rules provide the local meaning of logical constants. For example, a challenger chooses which conjunct to request, while a defender chooses a disjunct.
Structural rules determine how information is available across a play. This helps explain differences between intuitionistic and classical logic without changing the particle rules.
A terminal win in one play does not establish validity. Validity is connected to a proponent strategy that defeats every permitted opponent response.
The Formal Rule makes the standard framework asymmetric and supports an internal account of formality: the proponent cannot introduce an unendorsed atomic statement.
Immanent Reasoning responds to objections about hidden reasons and lack of content by making local reasons, formation, and some material commitments explicit.
summaries.why_it_matters: Dialogical logic offers a distinctive philosophical picture of logic: meaning is connected to use, commitments, challenges, and defences rather than being explained only from an external model-theoretic viewpoint. It provides a way to compare logical systems by examining how their interaction rules differ. At the same time, the source describes important objections, especially whether the standard games contain enough content and whether they are fully dialogical. Developments such as Immanent Reasoning show how the framework can be revised to address those questions.

important_terms.definition: A dialogue-based approach in which the meaning of logical expressions is described through permitted interaction between players.
Rules governing challenges and defences associated with particular logical expressions, such as conjunction, implication, or quantification.
Rules governing the general organization of a play, including its beginning, turn-taking, repetition limits, and ending.
The level of individual legal sequences of moves, where interaction and the use of logical expressions are displayed.
The level at which all possible plays are considered, especially to determine whether a player can win regardless of the opponent’s choices.
A complete conditional plan that specifies a player’s response to every relevant move by the opponent.
The standard restriction that the proponent may state an atomic formula only if the opponent has already stated it.
The view that different logics can be represented and compared by altering structural rules or adding logical operators.

questions_to_think_about: Why might the same particle rules support different logics when the structural rules change?
Does a dialogue-based account of meaning avoid truth-based semantics, or does it require some additional framework?
Is a restriction on introducing new atomic statements a useful account of formal reasoning?
What is gained by representing reasons explicitly inside a dialogue?
Can a winning strategy be understood as a proof, and what important features of interaction might that comparison leave out?

summaries.example: Suppose a debate is about this claim: “If a school club has both a science project and an art project, then it has a science project.” The proponent states the claim. The opponent challenges the “if” by stating its first part: “The club has both projects.” The proponent may then challenge the word “both” by asking for the science part. The opponent must provide that part, and the proponent can provide the conclusion. The exact moves are not just conversation habits; they are rules that give the logical words their meaning. If the opponent had asked for the art part instead, the dialogue might develop differently.
summaries.summary: Dialogical logic treats reasoning as a structured game between two players. The proponent puts forward a thesis, and the opponent challenges it. A move may be a statement, a request, a challenge, or a defence. The framework has two main kinds of rules. Particle rules explain how logical expressions work during interaction. For example, when someone states a conjunction, the other player can request either part; when someone states a disjunction, the defender chooses which part to give. Structural rules control the overall game: how it begins, whose turn it is, how often a move may be challenged, and when someone has no legal move left. The source emphasizes a difference between the play level and the strategy level. Winning one play is not the same as having a winning strategy, which must succeed against every possible opponent move. In the standard tradition, the Formal Rule limits the proponent’s use of atomic statements to those already stated by the opponent. This gives the system a particular account of formality. Other rule systems can represent intuitionistic, classical, modal, and other logics. Later proposals, including Immanent Reasoning, try to make reasons and the content of statements more visible.
key_ideas: The approach grew from the older idea that philosophical problems can be explored through question-and-answer exchanges.
A dialogue has two players with opposite roles, although the source notes that some scholars discuss whether cooperation can also fit the framework.
The rules for logical words are different from the rules that organize the whole game.
The meaning of a logical expression is connected to the actions it permits in the dialogue.
A player can win a particular round by luck, but a winning strategy must handle every possible choice by the opponent.
Changing the organizing rules can produce different logics while keeping the local rules for logical words.
summaries.why_it_matters: Dialogical logic makes the process of reasoning easier to see. Instead of treating logic as only a set of finished formulas, it asks what people are allowed to say, ask for, and use at each stage. This helps explain why two logical systems may use the same words but organize information differently. It also raises useful questions about whether formal logic contains enough real content and whether giving reasons should be part of the formal rules.

important_terms.definition: A way to study reasoning through conversations in which people follow rules for questioning and answering.
The statement that the whole dialogue is about.
The player who presents and supports the thesis.
The player who tests the thesis by raising challenges.
A rule for how a particular logical word can be challenged or defended.
A rule for organizing the dialogue, such as deciding turns, repetition, or how a play finishes.
A full plan for responding successfully to every possible move the other player could make.

questions_to_think_about: Why might the meaning of “and” be explained by asking what can be requested from a statement using “and”?
What is the difference between challenging a statement and defending it?
Why does a strategy need to consider choices the opponent has not yet made?
Could a rule that is fair to one player be unfair to the other? Why might that matter?
Would a dialogue feel complete if nobody could ask for reasons for simple facts?
